studies.meaning: She is told to enter the hall, sees what she takes for standing water, and gathers her clothing to wade. The floor is glass. When the illusion breaks she says nothing about the architecture; she says she has wronged herself, and submits. Commentators notice the sequence. The throne test produced a careful answer, and this much smaller trick produces surrender. What moves her is the discovery that her own eyes reported to her confidently and were wrong.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah keeps building scenes in which a sign is misread and then corrected, for an audience that had been asking for wonders. No occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah. Later storytelling filled the palace scene with a great deal of detail the Quran does not supply; the classical commentators note those additions as material from outside the text and do not build on them.

keyTerms.note: A tall polished structure. The word occurs in only two other passages of the Quran, both of them Pharaoh ordering a tower built so that he can climb it and look for the God of Moses.
Occurs once in the Quran. It means water with depth, the kind whose bottom you cannot see, which is precisely the judgement she makes and precisely the judgement that turns out to be wrong.

The root means putting a thing where it does not belong. Her confession is not that she broke a rule but that she misplaced something, which is how this Book generally describes worship aimed wrongly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water was the scarce thing. In a peninsula where wells were fought over and a caravan planned its stages around them, a floor of standing water inside a building would be a display of wealth no Arabian court could match. Her instinct to lift her hem is the instinct of someone who has waded through wadis after rain. The joke in the story is that there is no water at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the word for this hall four times altogether. Twice here, and twice in the mouth of Pharaoh, who orders one built so that he can climb up and look for the God of Moses. Both structures are attempts to reach something by construction. Only one of them stands in a story that ends with someone submitting.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Her confession puts the fault in herself before it says anything about God, and the order is the point. She does not argue that she was deceived, though she was. Submission arrives here as what happens when a person accepts that their reading of the evidence was both confident and mistaken, and a small domestic embarrassment does the work that letters and armies could not.

crossReferences.why: The hoopoe's first report of a queen with a mighty throne, which this scene finally answers.
Pharaoh orders a hall of the same name built for the opposite purpose, to disprove Moses.
Repeats that order in another surah, so the word carries a second and arrogant history.

studies.applyIt: Recall the last time you were completely certain and completely wrong about something small. Not a moral failure, just a misread. Sit for a moment with how sure you felt then, because the feeling was identical to the one you have now about something else entirely. You do not need to name which thing. Notice only that the sensation itself proves nothing.

studies.title: Why Hasten The Worse
studies.meaning: Salih is sent to Thamud with a single instruction, and the community splits into two parties and begins arguing before anything else happens. His reply does not address the split. He asks why they are in a hurry for the bad outcome while the good one is still available, and names the way back: seek forgiveness, and mercy becomes possible. The word for possibility stays in place. He offers them an open door, not a guaranteed result.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah running four prophet narratives in sequence. Thamud were a northern Arabian people whose rock-cut dwellings stood along the trade road to Syria, and Meccan caravans passed the site. The commentators report no specific occasion for these ayat. Their force comes from the setting: a warning about a vanished people, delivered to traders who had seen the empty facades with their own eyes.

keyTerms.note: A dual form, so the division is exactly two ways rather than many. The ayah reports it as the immediate effect of the message, arriving before any argument has been made on either side.
A verb of demanding something sooner than it is due. It returns later in this same surah in the mouths of the Prophet's own objectors, which quietly ties the two situations together.
A particle of hope rather than of guarantee. It stops the sentence short of promising that asking forgiveness produces mercy automatically, while still making mercy the whole point of the request.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The ruins of Thamud were not legend to the first hearers. Carved facades stood beside the northern caravan route, and traders from Mecca camped within sight of them on the way to Syria. Arabian poetry already used the place as shorthand for a people given more than most who left nothing behind but stonework. The surah is naming somewhere its audience could point to on a journey.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb Salih uses for hurrying toward harm returns later in this same surah, at ayah 72, where it is the surah's own contemporary objectors who are told that some of what they are rushing may already be close behind them. The same impatience is put in two mouths separated by centuries, and answered the same way both times.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are held together here that usually get separated. The passage is unambiguous that a bad outcome is coming, and equally unambiguous that it is not yet fixed. Seeking forgiveness appears not as a way of earning mercy but as the act that keeps the situation open. What gets ruled out is the assumption behind the demand: that the timetable is settled and nothing said now could matter.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same Thamud narrative at length, including the she-camel and the outcome only summarised here.
Gives Salih's appeal in its fullest form, with the same call to seek forgiveness and turn.
Puts the identical verb of hurrying into the mouth of the surah's contemporary audience.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you are rushing a bad outcome because waiting is uncomfortable. People do this constantly: forcing a conversation to its worst version, sending the resignation, saying the unrecoverable thing, because suspense costs more than damage does. Name one situation where you are doing that, and give it one more week. Nothing else is required. Just the week.

studies.title: Your Omen Is With God
studies.meaning: They tell Salih that he and those with him have brought bad luck on the town. He does not deny that things have gone badly. He relocates the cause: whatever bird of fortune they imagine is following them belongs with God, and what looks like misfortune is a test they are standing inside. The narrative then names nine men who were corrupting the city, which answers the accusation without arguing it. The trouble had a source, and it was local.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Reading the future from the flight of birds was an established Arabian practice, and the surah's audience knew the vocabulary precisely. Travellers would startle a bird and watch which way it flew before deciding whether to continue. No occasion is reported for these ayat; the commentators read the exchange as typical of what messengers met, and the first hearers would have recognised their own idiom quoted back at them.

keyTerms.gloss: we take you as an omen
keyTerms.note: Built from the word for bird, and occurring only here in this form. It preserves a whole practice of reading fortune from the direction a startled bird took before a journey began.
Salih repeats their own word back and reassigns it. Elsewhere the Quran uses the same term for the record of what a person has done, fastened to them rather than flying loose.
A word for fewer than ten men bound by blood. It occurs three times in the Quran, twice of a prophet's protective relatives and once, here, of a gang working against one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Omens governed ordinary decisions. Before setting out, a man might flush a bird from cover and read the direction it took as permission or as warning, and the practice had its own technical vocabulary. This was not superstition at the edge of life; it was part of how a caravan decided to leave on one day rather than another. Salih's answer does not mock the practice. It moves the authority behind it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the gang of nine appears only three times in the whole Quran. The other two are in a single exchange in surah 11, where Shuayb's opponents tell him that nothing but his kinsmen keeps him from being stoned. The same term covers the small band that shields a prophet and the small band that plots against one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply concedes the events and disputes the reading of them. Bad things did happen, and the passage does not pretend otherwise; it denies that they carry a message a community can decode by watching birds or by blaming a preacher. Calling the situation a test makes them participants rather than victims of chance, and it removes the middle layer of powers people had spent generations negotiating with.

crossReferences.why: Another town accuses its messengers of bringing bad luck and receives almost exactly this answer.
Uses the same word for omen to mean the record of a person's own deeds instead.
Holds the only other use of the word for a small kin band, protecting rather than plotting.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the moment you blame one person for a run of bad weeks. It is a comfortable move, because it gives the trouble a face and therefore a solution. Before you say it aloud, ask yourself what you would have to look at if that person were removed and the difficulty stayed exactly where it is.

studies.title: An Oath Sworn To Lie
studies.meaning: The plot is quoted in full, and its shape is what the ayah wants seen. They bind themselves to each other by an oath in God's name, agree to fall on the prophet and his household by night, and then rehearse in advance the sentence they will give to the next of kin, including a closing claim that they are telling the truth. The lie is drafted before the killing. So is the denial that follows it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The narrative belongs to Thamud, whose ruins lay on the northern caravan route. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah, and its placement matters more than any occasion would. The surah is speaking into a Mecca where hostility toward the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was hardening, and where a plot against him would later be described in strikingly similar language.

keyTerms.note: A reciprocal form, so the oath runs between them rather than up to a judge. It occurs once in the Quran. Each man is guaranteeing his silence to the others, which is what makes such a group hard to break.
From the word for passing the night somewhere. The verb carries the whole idea of a raid under cover of dark, and the emphatic ending turns a proposal into a vow.
The emphatic form of the word for truthful. Placing it inside a rehearsed lie is the sharpest stroke in the ayah, since the claim to honesty is scripted alongside the falsehood it protects.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blood was answered by blood, and the answer was owed to the guardian of the victim's line. That is exactly why the plotters rehearse what to tell him. A killing without a claimant went unpunished, and an alibi sworn by nine men was very hard to overturn. Night raids were the standard method precisely because they left nobody able to testify. Every element of this plan was ordinary practice.
studies.didYouKnow: The reciprocal verb for swearing to one another occurs only once in the Quran, here. The oath is taken in God's name, and the sentence it is protecting ends with the plotters calling themselves truthful. The answer comes in the very next ayah, which uses a single word for scheming four times in one short line.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An oath in God's name is used to seal a murder and a perjury, and the passage reports it without any comment at all. Nothing is said about the oath being void. The answer comes instead in the next line, where the planning is matched and outmatched. The response to religious language used as cover is not an argument here but an outcome, narrated quickly and without heat.

crossReferences.why: Describes a plot against the Prophet in the same vocabulary of planning met by planning.
The immediate answer to this oath, and the outcome of the plan they swore to.
States that schemes of this kind were already known and accounted for, however large they looked.

studies.applyIt: Listen this week for the phrases people use to certify themselves: honestly, to be fair, I swear. Notice how often one arrives just before something shaky. Then listen for the same habit in your own speech. The point is not to stop saying it. It is to hear the small pressure that makes you reach for a guarantee.

studies.title: They Planned And God Planned
studies.meaning: Four lines close the story. The plot is answered by a counter-plan the plotters never notice, the outcome arrives, and the reader is directed to the ruins rather than to the destruction. The empty houses are the sign, and they are addressed to people who know things. The last line is the shortest of all: those who believed and guarded themselves were brought out safely. The rescue is given one sentence and no detail whatever.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah that repeats this structure across several narratives. The rock-cut dwellings of Thamud still stood on the route north from Mecca toward Syria in the seventh century, and stand today. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat. The audience is pointed at physical evidence they could visit rather than at a report they would have to accept on someone's authority.

keyTerms.note: The root covers planning that works through concealment. The line uses it four times in one short sentence, twice of the plotters and twice of God, so the reply is deliberately given the offence's own name.
From the root for a heel, or for whatever comes along behind. The word names not the result of an act but the thing that trails it, which is why this Book uses it so often for how a story finishes.
A word for something emptied from within. It is used elsewhere of a village fallen on its roofs and of toppled palm trunks, and it describes a structure that still holds its shape.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ruins were part of the landscape and part of the poetry. A pre-Islamic ode traditionally opened with the poet halting at an abandoned campsite to read what was left: ashes, tent pegs, a ring of stones. Arabian audiences were trained to find meaning in the traces a departed community left behind. These ayat use that habit exactly as it stands, and simply change what the traces are evidence of.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for scheming appears four times in a single line here, twice for the plotters and twice for God, and the surah reaches for it twice more before it ends. The word describing the empty houses occurs five times in the Quran and always of a structure that kept its shape. Nothing in these lines describes the destruction itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: One word covers what the plotters did and what God did, and the whole difference is placed in the outcome rather than in the vocabulary. The classical commentators are careful at this point: the shared term marks correspondence, not likeness of nature. What is being claimed is that concealment confers no advantage, because the only party who can be genuinely unobserved is not among the schemers.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same paired vocabulary of planning, closing with the statement that God is the best of planners.
Uses the same word for hollowed houses in a general statement about towns ruined for wrongdoing.
Narrates the destruction of Thamud directly, where here only the aftermath is shown.

studies.applyIt: Walk past something that closed: a shop, a building site that stopped, a house someone moved out of. Look at it for a minute longer than is comfortable. These ayat ask their audience to read a place rather than accept a claim, and the exercise still works. There is nothing to conclude at the end of it. Just look properly.

studies.title: The Answer Of His People
studies.meaning: Lot's question is asked twice, and the second form names what he is asking about. The stress falls on openness rather than concealment: the phrase about seeing describes a community acting in front of one another without shame. His charge is ignorance, which in the Quran's usage means recklessness rather than lack of information. The third line is where the passage arrives. They do not answer the charge. They move to expel the man who made it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, one of four prophet narratives set side by side in this surah. The Lot story was widely known in Arabia through Jewish and Christian neighbours and through ruined sites near the Dead Sea on the Syrian road. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. The surah's interest lies in the pattern of the response, which is why the reply is quoted at length and the conduct is not described.

keyTerms.note: A verb of sight used for perception and for open acknowledgement. Commentators read it either as acting within sight of one another, or as acting in full awareness of what the act is.
From a root this Book opposes not to knowledge but to forbearance. It describes acting rashly against what one already knows, which is why it can be said to people who are perfectly informed.
A verb of purification, used here as a sneer. The identical accusation appears in one other place in the Quran, in exactly these words, which suggests it was remembered as their characteristic reply.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Expulsion was the heaviest sanction a town could impose. Outside the settlement a man had no water rights, no protection on the road, and nobody obliged to answer for his blood. Driving out a household was not a gesture but a sentence. The reply quoted here is therefore not rhetoric. It is a community reaching for the strongest instrument it possessed, and aiming it at the person naming its conduct.
studies.didYouKnow: The sneer that closes this passage appears twice in the Quran, in surah 7 and here, in exactly the same words: they are people who keep themselves pure. The two versions differ only in whom they name for expulsion, one naming Lot's household and the other his followers generally. It is one of several places where this surah restates an earlier account with a single detail altered.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The weight falls on the response rather than on the offence. A community is told plainly what it is doing, and its answer is to remove the man who said so, on the grounds that he and his household are too clean to live beside. This is presented as the recurring shape of rejection across the prophetic narratives: not a counter-argument, but the expulsion of whoever makes the standard visible.

crossReferences.why: The parallel account, closing with the identical sneer about people who keep themselves pure.
Gives Lot's appeal at greater length within that surah's long series of messengers and peoples.
Adds the visiting messengers and Lot's distress, which this compressed account leaves out entirely.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last time someone named something uncomfortable about a group you belong to: a workplace, a family, a group chat. Recall what happened to that person afterwards. Not what was said about the substance of it, but what happened to them. Notice whether you joined in, stayed quiet, or made a little room for them.

studies.title: The One Who Stayed Behind
studies.meaning: The Lot narrative ends in three strokes. The household is brought out, one member is not, and a rain falls that the passage declines to call anything but rain. The word used for her is not a word for punishment; it means one who remained, and the Quran uses it of her without ever describing what she did. Then the surah turns. The run of prophet narratives closes with praise, with peace on those God selected, and with the question the rest of the surah will press.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Four narratives have run in sequence and this is the seam between them and what follows. The line about praise and peace closes the storytelling and opens the long series of questions. Commentators report no occasion for these ayat. What the audience had in front of them was a set of ruined places along their own trade routes and a message saying the same pattern was in progress around them.

keyTerms.note: From a root for remaining or lagging. The Quran uses this word seven times and every one belongs to this single episode, describing the member of the household who did not leave with the rest.

The ordinary word for rainfall, given with no adjective at all. The clause after it supplies the judgement rather than the noun, which leaves the event itself described in the plainest possible terms.
A verb for picking out the pure part of something. It is used of prophets and of a few others, so the peace pronounced here rests on people God singled out rather than on merit anyone claimed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rain in Arabia was the good news of the year. A season's rainfall decided whether a family's animals lived, whether the wells refilled, and whether the tribe moved. Poets celebrated it and travellers watched the horizon for it. To make rain the instrument of ruin was to invert the most reliable blessing the audience knew, and the second line says so with one dry comment.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the one who stayed behind occurs seven times in the Quran, and all seven belong to this same episode, spread across five surahs. The Quran never states what she did. It names only her position, that she remained, and leaves the rest of the account to a silence the classical commentators largely kept as well.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Rescue is shown running along a line other than household membership. Belonging to a prophet's family saves nobody in this account, and the exception is stated without being explained, which stops it from hardening into a formula. The praise that follows then reframes the whole sequence of narratives. What has been recounted is not a series of disasters but the record of a selection.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same exception in the same word, spoken by the messengers before the town is reached.
Names two prophets' wives as a general case, so closeness to a prophet is not itself protection.
Runs the same rescue pattern for Noah, where the household divides along a different line.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your sense of standing on safe ground comes from the company you keep: your family's reputation, your circle, the group you would be counted among. That is not a bad thing to have. But spend one quiet minute asking what would still be true of you if none of it were attached to your name.

studies.title: Trees You Could Not Grow
studies.meaning: The surah changes mode here. Instead of narrating it begins asking, and each question sets a familiar fact beside an impossible rival. Who made the sky and the earth and sends down the water that becomes orchards? Then the sting: you could not have grown a single one of those trees. The point is not that a creator exists. It is that the audience already depends on someone daily and has never once been able to do the essential part themselves.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the final third of a surah that has just finished four prophet narratives. Commentators report no occasion for this ayah. The Meccan audience was not atheist. They acknowledged a creator and attached partners to him for the ordinary business of life, which is why these questions are framed as comparisons rather than as proofs. They ask which of two accounts fits what the hearers were already doing.

keyTerms.note: Enclosed and planted ground rather than wild growth. The word appears three times in the Quran, and the other two sit in short lists of what has been grown, one of them among the promises of the garden.
Occurs once in the Quran. It means beauty that pleases the eye specifically, so the ayah credits God not only with the harvest but with the fact that an orchard is a pleasant place to stand in.
The causative verb for making something sprout. Putting it in the second person and then denying it carries the whole argument: the farmer does everything except the one part that matters.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Date palms took years to bear and were counted, taxed and inherited individually. A man in an oasis town could name the trees his grandfather planted. Everyone understood the labour of it: clearing, walling, irrigating, pollinating by hand. And everyone understood the limit. You could do all of it and lose the crop, or do none of it and watch a seedling come up anyway. The ayah puts its finger exactly there.
studies.didYouKnow: The refrain that closes this ayah occurs five times in the Quran and all five are in this surah, packed into ayat 60 through 64. Nowhere else does the Quran ask the question in these words. The term used here for gardens that are a delight to look at occurs only this once in the whole Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument works from participation rather than from first causes. It does not ask anyone to reason back to a beginning; it asks them to notice that they are already inside a process they contribute to and cannot complete. That places the claim within reach of a farmer and a merchant equally. And the closing comment is about equating rather than denying, which names the actual error being addressed.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same challenge about sowing directly, asking who it is that makes the seed grow.
Runs a longer list of what was grown from the same water, ending with walled gardens.
Continues the same series of questions, moving from rainfall to navigation and to wind.

studies.applyIt: Eat something today that grew, and before you start, work out how much of it you could have produced yourself from the beginning. Not bought, produced. Most people get about as far as digging a hole. It is a small exercise and it takes a minute, and it puts the ayah's question into your own hands.

studies.title: The Ground That Holds Still
studies.meaning: Four verbs of making, one after another, all with the same subject. The earth is set as a place to settle on, rivers are run through it, mountains are fixed on it, and a barrier is placed between two bodies of water. Commentators read the barrier as the line where fresh and salt water meet without freely mixing. Every item is something the audience stood on or drank from, and the question arrives after the list rather than before it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has moved from stories to questions and this is the second in the run. No occasion of revelation is reported. The audience lived where the ground was the one dependable thing in an unstable arrangement: tribes shifted, caravans failed, rain came or did not come. Naming the earth's steadiness as a decision rather than a given is the pressure the ayah applies.

keyTerms.note: From the root for staying still. The word means somewhere you can come to rest, so the claim concerns the earth being habitable rather than the earth being motionless in space.
From a root used of a ship's anchor and of anything that holds fast. The image is of weights set to steady something, which is how this Book usually introduces mountains into a list.
Occurs once in the Quran. It names something set between two parties to keep them apart, used in Arabic of a screen or a wall rather than of a natural boundary in a landscape.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had almost no permanent rivers. What it had were wadis that ran hard for a day after rain and were dry beds again within the week. A hearer would picture that sudden torrent, not a great river. And along the coast, sailors knew precisely where drinkable water ended and the sea began, because staying alive on a long stage depended on knowing it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the barrier between the two waters occurs only here in the Quran. The same meeting of waters is described twice more, in surahs 25 and 55, and both of those use a different word for the boundary. Three passages describe one phenomenon, and no two of them reach for the same term.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The list is made entirely of stable things, and stability is precisely what is being attributed. A world that stays put long enough to be farmed, navigated and inherited is presented as an act rather than as a background condition. That claim carries a second one inside it. Whatever else is uncertain in a person's life, the arrangement they are standing on was arranged, and it holds.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same two waters meeting with a boundary that neither of them crosses.
Names the same phenomenon again, calling the boundary a partition rather than a barrier.
Pairs the earth as a resting place with the mountains as pegs, in that same order.

studies.applyIt: Stand still outdoors for one minute today and give your attention to the ground rather than to anything on it. The point of the ayah is that the reliable things are the ones you stopped noticing years ago. You will not feel anything dramatic. Notice instead that you have never once had to wonder whether it would hold.

studies.title: The One Driven To A Corner
studies.meaning: This is one of a run of questions, each closing with the same challenge about whether any other god exists alongside God. The others point at creation. This one points at rescue, and the person it describes is precise: not someone in difficulty but someone compelled, out of options, with nothing left to try. Then the sentence turns unexpectedly and adds succession on the earth to the list, so the handing of the world from one generation to the next is counted among the things nobody else supplies.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the argument that follows the surah's prophet narratives. Five questions run in sequence, each contrasting what God does with the complete inactivity of what the Meccans invoked beside Him. The community was under sustained pressure at this stage. The commentators note that the Meccans themselves called on God directly in emergencies at sea and in the desert, while keeping other objects of worship for ordinary business.

keyTerms.note: A passive form from a root meaning harm and constraint: someone pushed into a position, not merely suffering. The same word governs the Quran's language about necessity, where choice has effectively run out.
The verb for pulling a covering off something. Harm is pictured as a cloth laid over a person rather than a thing done to them, so relief is described as removal rather than repair.
The plural of one who comes after another and takes their place. It carries both inheritance and responsibility, and the Quran uses it of humanity holding the earth in turn, never permanently.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Desert travel had a narrow margin. Wells were days apart and known by name, and a party that missed one, or found it fouled, could be finished within a day. Custom offered a formula for danger: a person under threat could call out the name of a tribe and claim its protection, and the tribe's honour was engaged by the call. The passage borrows that structure and removes the intermediary.
studies.didYouKnow: Five ayat in a row here, from sixty to sixty-four, are built to one pattern. Each opens with the same interrogative particle, sets out something only God does, and closes with an identical three-word challenge about another god beside God. Only the clause after that challenge changes, moving through equating, not knowing, scarcely remembering, God being far above what they set beside Him, and finally a demand for evidence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument for one God is made from memory rather than from doctrine. It points at a moment the listener has already had and asks who was addressed in it, which is a different kind of case from the ones built on the order of the heavens. There is a promise embedded in the question as well, that the call of the desperate is answered, though the text does not specify what the answer will look like.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same question from God's side: I am near, and I answer the caller when he calls.
Describes the storm at sea where every other object of appeal is forgotten and only God is called.
Gives a worked instance, the call from inside the darkness and the deliverance that followed it.

studies.applyIt: Remember the last time you were genuinely out of options, and recall what you actually said, in whatever words came. Say the same thing again now, deliberately, while nothing is wrong. The passage locates God at the end of the human rope. Saying the words when you are not at the end tests whether the address was to God or to the emergency.

studies.title: Winds Sent Before The Rain
studies.meaning: The questions move outdoors and into the dark. Who gets you through when you cannot see, on land or at sea, and who sends the winds ahead of rain? The second half is precise. The winds are not the mercy; they are what runs in front of it. Commentators note that both halves describe help arriving before it is needed, once as the ability to find a road at night and once as advance notice that water is on its way.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, midway through the surah's sequence of questions. Meccans travelled for a living, north in summer and south in winter, and navigated by stars across country that had no roads at all. Coastal trade ran along the Red Sea. No occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah. It is aimed at an audience whose survival had repeatedly depended on both of the things it names.

keyTerms.note: A plural, so the phrase is darknesses rather than darkness. The Quran uses the plural for conditions where nothing can be made out and a person depends entirely on something outside their own sight.
From the root of good news and of a face brightening at it. The word turns the wind into a messenger rather than a force, arriving with information ahead of the thing it announces.
Here the word stands for the rain itself, a usage this Book repeats elsewhere. Calling the water mercy and the wind its herald puts an entire weather system into the vocabulary of relationship.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Desert navigation was a learned craft. Guides read star positions, dune shapes and the feel of the air, and a caravan that lost its guide could wander until the water ran out. At sea, sailors kept the coast in sight for the same reason. And the wind that came up before rain was the one reliable early warning in a landscape where a flash flood could fill a wadi within minutes.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about winds sent as heralds before God's mercy appears three times in the Quran, in surahs 7 and 25 and here, in almost identical wording. In the other two places it stands as a statement. Here it is turned into a question, which is what this stretch of the surah does to material stated plainly elsewhere.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Both halves of the ayah are about not being left to work things out alone. Guidance in the dark and warning before a storm are one act described in two settings, and neither is earned or requested anywhere in the sentence. The closing formula then raises God above association rather than merely denying the partners, which shifts the correction from a dispute about facts to a question of proportion.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing about the winds as a plain declaration, and continues to the rain.
Repeats the wind and mercy phrase, followed by the sending down of pure water.
Names the stars as the means of finding a way through darkness on land and sea.

studies.applyIt: Think of a decision from the last year where you could not see far ahead and it worked out anyway. Not a lucky escape, an ordinary one. Write the sentence describing it. Most people find they have several of these and have never counted them, because a road that turns out fine leaves no memory of the dark.

studies.title: Bring Your Proof
studies.meaning: The last question in the series is the one the audience actually objected to. Who begins the creation and then repeats it, and who feeds you from sky and earth? The two halves are joined deliberately. The second was agreed, the first was denied, and the ayah treats them as one act. Then the demand switches direction. Bring your evidence. The burden lands on the objection rather than on the claim, which is where this whole run has been heading.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Resurrection was the part of the message Mecca found least credible, and objections to it recur through the ayat immediately following this one. The commentators report no specific occasion. The position of the ayah at the close of the run of questions is itself the argument: everything already conceded in the previous lines is being used to make the disputed part reasonable.

keyTerms.note: A verb for doing something the first time. Paired with the verb for repeating, it presents the raising as a second run of a process rather than as a separate and stranger kind of act.
A word for decisive evidence rather than for argument or opinion. The phrase demanding it occurs four times in the Quran, always put to people asserting something about God without grounds.
The verb for supplying what sustains life: food, rain, and everything that arrives without being manufactured. This is the half of the ayah that nobody in the original audience was disputing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca grew almost nothing. It lived on trade and on what came in, which meant everyone in the valley understood provision as something that arrived rather than something produced. Caravans came up from Yemen and down from Syria, and the city's entire economy rested on goods it had not made and water it had not found. The ayah's second question was not an abstraction there.
studies.didYouKnow: The demand to produce your proof occurs four times in the Quran, and one of the other three stands in the very next surah, addressed on the Day of Judgement to communities asked to justify what they had claimed. The phrase is always put to the objector and never to the messenger, in all four places.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Resurrection is argued here by analogy rather than by assertion. If a first making happened, a second is not a different order of difficulty, and the passage does not press further than that. The closing demand then sets the standard for the whole dispute. Denial is treated as a claim like any other, requiring grounds, which quietly refuses the position that doubt costs nothing to hold.

crossReferences.why: States the same point directly, that repeating the creation is easier, and the highest description is His.
Puts the identical demand for proof on the Day of Judgement, when an answer is finally due.
Answers the objection about crumbled bones with the same appeal to the first origination.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you dismiss something quickly, and ask what you would produce if someone asked you for grounds. Not whether you are right. Just what you would actually put on the table. Most confident dismissals turn out to rest on a feeling and a sample of one, and it is worth knowing which of yours do.

studies.title: No One Knows But God
studies.meaning: The statement is absolute and it is placed in the messenger's own mouth. Nobody in the heavens or the earth knows the unseen except God, and the second clause narrows to the case in dispute: they have no perception of when they will be raised. Commentators note that the first clause takes in angels and prophets without exception. The surah has just spent many ayat showing what creatures can know. This is where the line gets drawn.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah opened with a bird carrying news nobody else had and a court that could move a throne across a distance, and now it closes off the category those wonders might have suggested. No occasion is reported for the ayah. Its audience included people who paid soothsayers for hidden knowledge, and the statement removes that whole market at once, beginning with the Prophet himself.

keyTerms.note: What is absent from perception rather than what is mysterious. The definite form makes it a single domain, so the exception at the end of the sentence covers all of it and not merely parts.
An interrogative the Quran uses only of the Hour and the raising. Its narrowness matters, since the ayah denies knowledge of the timing specifically and not knowledge that the event is coming.
A verb of perceiving by feel or intuition rather than by learning. Denying it rules out the hunch along with the report, which is the harder half of what the clause claims.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Soothsayers were a paid profession. People consulted them about lost camels, marriage prospects, and whether a raid would succeed, and the good ones built reputations that carried across tribes. Claimed access to hidden news was a livelihood and a form of standing. An ayah placing the unseen wholly out of reach was not a philosophical point in that setting. It was an economic one.
studies.didYouKnow: The final clause of this ayah appears word for word in one other place, in surah 16, where it describes the idols themselves as dead and unaware of when they will be raised. Here the identical words are applied to the people who worship them. The interrogative in that clause occurs six times in the Quran, always about the timing of the Hour.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A clean boundary is drawn between the Creator and everything created, and it runs across knowledge rather than across power. Prophethood is defined by what is given rather than by what is possessed: a prophet reports what he has been told and does not have a window onto the rest. That keeps the message from being confused with fortune telling, and it leaves the future genuinely open for the reader.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same question about timing, saying the knowledge of it rests with God alone.
Lists specific things held back, ending with what a person will earn tomorrow.
Says the unseen is not disclosed except to a messenger God chooses, and then only in part.

studies.applyIt: Count how many times today you predict something out loud: how a meeting will go, what someone will say, whether the thing will work. Just count them, do not stop yourself. By evening the number will surprise you, and so will how few of the predictions you thought to go back and check.

studies.title: Knowledge That Ran Out
studies.meaning: Three corrections in a row, each opening with the same particle, and each one heavier than the last. Their knowledge about the hereafter has run out, or has caught up with itself and come to nothing; then they are in doubt about it; then they are blind to it altogether. Commentators read the progression as deliberate, moving from a claim about information to a claim about capacity. The verb in the first clause is rare, and they discuss its form at length without settling on one rendering.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, placed immediately after the statement that no one knows the unseen. The connection is the argument itself: since the timing is closed to everyone, the confident denials being voiced in Mecca are not knowledge either. No occasion of revelation is reported. The ayah belongs to a stretch of the surah dealing directly with the objection that resurrection is an old and worn out story.

keyTerms.note: A rare verb from the root of overtaking. Commentators read it as their knowledge failing them, or as it arriving all at once and too late, and they record the range rather than settling it.
The state of holding two possibilities without weighing either one. It sits between the first clause and the third as the middle stage, which is exactly why the ayah does not stop there.
The plural of a word for blindness used of the heart rather than of the eye. It names an inability rather than an opinion, which makes it the heaviest of the three descriptions.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian argument prized the flat repeated correction. A poet or a disputant would knock down a claim and then knock down the improved version, stacking rebuttals in the same shape so that an audience felt the escalation before it weighed the content. This ayah uses that structure exactly, three times inside one short line, and the first hearers would have recognised the rhythm immediately.
studies.didYouKnow: The same particle of correction opens all three clauses of this ayah, one directly after another. The line has fourteen words in Arabic and three of them are that single particle. The verb in the first clause is written in the standard copies with an unusual spelling, and the classical commentaries devote considerable space to working out what it carries.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates three positions that people usually blur together: not knowing, doubting, and being unable to see. Only the third is treated as a condition rather than a stance, and the ayah arrives there last, having ruled out the milder descriptions first. That order matters. It refuses to call honest uncertainty blindness, and it refuses to call a settled refusal honest uncertainty.

crossReferences.why: Says it is not the eyes that go blind but the hearts inside the chests.
Reports the same wavering about the Hour, phrased as guessing rather than as knowing.
Immediately precedes this, closing off the knowledge that would have settled the question.

studies.applyIt: Try saying honestly which of the three the ayah describes fits you, on some question you have been avoiding. Not the religious version necessarily. Any question at all. There is a real difference between not having looked into it, genuinely weighing it, and not wanting to see it, and nobody but you can tell which you are doing.

studies.title: Nothing But Old Stories
studies.meaning: The objection is quoted with its reasoning intact. We and our fathers will be dust, this promise has been made before and nothing came of it, so it is old storytelling. Two answers follow. The first sends them out to look at what became of earlier communities, moving an argument about the future onto ground they can walk across. The second is not addressed to them at all. It tells the Prophet not to grieve and not to feel hemmed in by what they are plotting.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, where the surah turns from its questions to the objections themselves. The phrase they use, that this is nothing but legends of the ancients, occurs nine times in the Quran, always as Mecca's standing dismissal of the recitation. Commentators report no specific occasion for these ayat. The closing line, telling the Prophet not to grieve, points to a stage where rejection had become personally costly.

keyTerms.note: From the root for lines of writing. The taunt was that this material came out of books, which is why the Quran answers it elsewhere by pointing out that the reciter neither read nor wrote.

A physical narrowness used for an emotional state. The Arabic image is of space closing in rather than of sadness, which is a different and more exact description of what sustained pressure feels like.
An imperative to move through the land. This Book uses it repeatedly for one specific kind of evidence: looking at ruined places rather than reasoning from principles at home.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Meccan trade routes ran past a series of abandoned settlements, and merchants knew them as landmarks on a schedule. For two months of the year much of the city was on the road. An instruction to travel and look was not a metaphor for these hearers. It named an ordinary part of a working year, and the sites named earlier in this surah lay along the way.
studies.didYouKnow: The dismissal quoted here, that the recitation is nothing but legends of the ancients, appears nine times in the Quran, spread across nine different surahs. It is among the most frequently repeated objections in the whole Book, and it is always given in the objectors' own words rather than summarised by the narration.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply refuses to argue on the objection's own terms. Rather than proving the resurrection, it points at a pattern already visible in the world and lets the inference stand unspoken. Then it turns aside to the messenger, which is the more unusual move. The passage takes the strain of being disbelieved seriously enough to address it directly, without asking him to stop feeling it.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the same taunt about legends and describes the coverings placed over their hearing.
Gives the fullest version of the accusation, together with the answer that follows it.
Repeats the instruction not to grieve over them or be constricted by what they scheme.

studies.applyIt: If someone has dismissed something that matters to you, look at the second half of this passage. The reply given there is not a better argument. It is permission to stop carrying the weight of their refusal. Try setting one such refusal down for a single day. You can pick it up tomorrow. See what the day is like without it.

studies.title: Perhaps It Is Already Behind You
studies.meaning: A demand for a date is met with a sentence that supplies none. Perhaps part of what you are rushing has already come up at your heels: the verb pictures something riding directly behind, close enough to touch. Then two statements change the subject entirely. Your Lord is generous toward people, and most of them are not thankful. And He knows what their chests hold shut as well as what they announce. A threat is answered with an account of what is being withheld.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The question about timing recurs across this period, and it was rhetorical: demanding a date was a way of showing that none would be given. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat. The pairing that follows, of generosity with ingratitude, belongs to a stretch where the surah describes an audience receiving more time than it has any idea it is receiving.

keyTerms.note: From the word for the second rider on a camel, seated behind the saddle. The verb occurs once in the Quran, and it makes the coming thing near rather than merely certain at some point.
The root means excess, what is over and above what was owed. It names the gap between what people are given and what could fairly be required of them, which is the ayah's actual subject.
A verb for covering something over to protect it, used of a shelter. It suggests things held close for safekeeping rather than merely hidden, a gentler picture of a secret than the English carries.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Riding double was ordinary. On a raid or a long stage a second man sat behind the saddle, and the word for him was in daily use. The image of someone seated directly behind you, out of sight and moving at exactly your speed, was as familiar as a saddle strap. That is what the passage says about the thing the objectors were demanding to be shown.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for what may already be following occurs once in the Quran. It comes from the noun for the rider seated behind the saddle, and the only other appearance of that root describes ranks of angels arriving one behind another at a battle. Both usages are about something coming up close behind, unseen by the one in front.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Delay is reframed as favour rather than as absence. The passage does not defend the timetable; it observes that the objectors are standing inside a period of grace and reading it as evidence against the message. The closing line then shuts the exit, since what a person keeps covered is already known. The delay is therefore neither an oversight nor a shortage of information about who deserves what.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same demand for haste by noting that a day with your Lord is not measured as you measure.
Says an appointed term is what holds it back, and that it will arrive suddenly.
Puts the same verb of hurrying toward harm into the mouth of an earlier people.

studies.applyIt: Think of a consequence you have been expecting that has not arrived. Most people are carrying one. Rather than reading the delay as a sign it will never come, or as proof that you got away with it, try treating it for a week as time you were given. Then decide what you want to do with the week.

studies.title: A Clear Book Holds Everything
studies.meaning: Four short lines that widen and then narrow again. Nothing hidden anywhere stands outside a clear record. This recitation settles most of what the Children of Israel had been disputing among themselves. It is guidance and mercy, though the phrase is qualified, for those who believe. And judgement between them belongs to their Lord. Commentators note the restraint of that last line, which lifts the verdict out of human hands while the argument is still going on.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the close of the surah's long argument. Jewish and Christian communities were known to Mecca through trade and through settlements to the north and south, and their internal disagreements were not private. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. What is being made is a specific claim about what the recitation does, placed just before the surah turns toward its final scenes.

keyTerms.note: An unusual feminine form of the word for what is absent, occurring once in the Quran. The ending intensifies it, so the sense is closer to a deeply buried matter than to anything merely out of sight.
From the root for following a track. The verb means telling a story by tracing it forward, which is why the same root gives the word for the accounts of earlier prophets throughout this Book.
A reciprocal verb of disagreement, describing a dispute inside a single community rather than between two of them. It names precisely the situation this recitation is being said to address.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca sat on the road between two literate religious worlds. Merchants heard scripture read in Syrian churches and in Jewish settlements to the north and in Yemen, and the questions those communities argued over travelled north and south with the goods. An Arabian audience knew these were long disputed matters before they heard a recitation claiming to settle them, which is what gives this passage its edge.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a hidden thing in the first of these ayat occurs only here in the Quran, in a feminine form the language uses for intensification rather than for gender. The surah opened by describing a book that makes things clear, and it returns to that same phrase here, one clear record holding what nothing else can reach.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Three claims are stacked and the last one limits the first two. The record is complete, the recitation resolves disputes, and yet the resolving is not handed to anyone as a warrant. Guidance is described as arriving for those who receive it, and the verdict between disputing parties is explicitly kept with God. That combination is what stops a claim to clarity from turning into a licence to judge.

crossReferences.why: Opens the surah with the same description of a book that makes things clear.
Says the Children of Israel differed only after knowledge came, and that God will judge between them.
States that nothing falls or lies hidden without being in a clear record.

studies.applyIt: Find one disagreement you are in where you have been quietly certain that you will eventually be vindicated. Notice what the expectation of that verdict is costing you day to day. The last of these ayat hands the verdict elsewhere. Try acting for a week as though it has been handed elsewhere, and see what comes back.

studies.title: You Cannot Make Them Hear
studies.meaning: Two instructions that look unrelated belong together. Rely on God, because you stand on clear truth; and then, immediately, a limit. You cannot make the dead hear, and you cannot make the deaf hear a call once they have turned their backs and are walking away. Commentators read the second line as consolation rather than as despair. Failure to persuade is not the messenger's failure, because the thing being demanded of him was never within his power to produce.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the closing stretch of the surah. The pairing suggests a stage when the message had been public for years and refused, and the strain was landing on the one delivering it. No specific occasion is reported. These lines appear again in surah 30 in almost identical wording, so the same consolation was given more than once, in more than one setting.

keyTerms.note: A verb for handing a matter over to an agent. It does not mean stopping work. It means doing your own part and placing the outcome, which was never yours, with someone else.
This Book uses deafness for a refusal to take something in rather than for a physical condition, which is why the clause adds the detail of turning away and walking off.
A participle of showing the back. It adds motion to the picture: not a person standing and declining, but one already leaving, which is why the call cannot reach them at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A public caller had one instrument, the voice, and one setting, a crowd within earshot. Announcements were made at the market, at the pilgrimage season, at gatherings around the sanctuary. If a man got up and walked out, that was the end of it, because there was no way to reach him afterwards. The image in this ayah is drawn from what the Prophet was doing on ordinary days.
studies.didYouKnow: These lines occur twice in the Quran, here and in surah 30, in almost exactly the same words, with a single word spelled slightly differently in the second version. It is one of a small number of passages the Quran repeats nearly verbatim across surahs, and both times they sit near the close of a long argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is drawn tightly around the messenger. He is answerable for delivering and for reliance, and not for the result, which is placed outside the range of anything he can do. That keeps the message from becoming a measure of the messenger's worth, and it removes the temptation to force a response. What is left to him is accuracy and trust, in that order.

crossReferences.why: Repeats these two ayat almost word for word at the close of another Meccan argument.
States the same limit again, that you cannot make those in the graves hear.
Defines the role directly: you are a reminder, and not someone set over them.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person you have been trying to convince of something for a long time. Say the last line to yourself: they have turned, and they are walking. You are not being asked to stop caring or to think badly of them. You are being asked to stop measuring yourself by an outcome that was never yours to produce.

studies.title: The Ones Who Can Hear
studies.meaning: The limit is stated a third time and then turned around. You are not the one who guides the blind out of where they have wandered. The only people you can make listen are those who already believe in the signs, and the sentence ends by calling them submitters. Commentators note the direction of that clause: belief is not described as the result of hearing but as the condition that makes hearing possible, which reverses the usual order of persuasion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the same closing sequence as the ayah before it, and repeated in nearly identical form in surah 30. No specific occasion of revelation is reported. The setting is a mission that had been public for years, in a city where the arguments had all been made and positions had hardened, and where the question of why plain evidence was not working had become the live one.

keyTerms.note: The participle rather than the verb, so what is denied is the role and not only the act. This exact form occurs once in the Quran; the parallel in surah 30 uses a shorter spelling.
Blindness of the heart, matching the deafness in the previous ayah. The Quran pairs the two often, and both name an inability to receive rather than a punishment already imposed.
From the root of surrender and of peace. Placed at the end of the sentence, it describes what the listening ones already are rather than what they are being urged to become.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Guiding was a paid occupation. Across trackless country a caravan hired a man who knew the route, and the survival of the whole party rested on his sight and his memory. To say that someone is not a guide for the blind is to use a technical word from that trade. A guide could lead a man who could see the marks. He could not lend him his eyes.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a guide in this exact form occurs only once in the Quran, here. The near identical ayah in surah 30 uses a shorter spelling of the same word. The two passages run in parallel for two ayat and differ only in details of this kind, which is why the classical commentators discuss them side by side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is placed entirely outside human agency, and that hard saying is held together with an equally firm one, that the message must still be delivered. The two are not in tension here. Delivering is the work; the opening is not. What follows for a reader is a change in what counts as success, and a reason to stop treating someone else's refusal as a verdict on the truth.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing directly, that you do not guide whom you love but God guides.
Gives the parallel wording, with the same participle written in a shorter form.
Asks whether you would compel people, and says no soul believes except by leave.

studies.applyIt: Notice what happens in you when someone you care about does not see something obvious. There is usually a flare of frustration and then a plan to explain it better. Try naming the frustration for what it is: an attempt to do a job this ayah says is not yours. Then say the thing once, plainly, and let it sit.

studies.title: A Creature Out Of The Earth
studies.meaning: When the sentence falls due, a creature is brought out of the earth and speaks. What it says is reported in one clause: that people had not been holding the signs with certainty. Commentators differ widely over what this creature is and exactly when it appears, and they record the range without settling it. What the ayah itself supplies is narrow. Something emerges, it speaks, and the content of its speech concerns the state of human conviction rather than anything else.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the surah's closing sequence about the Day. The classical tradition treats this as one of the signs preceding the Hour, and reports about it vary considerably in their detail. The commentators are cautious at this point, and observe that the Quran supplies almost nothing beyond the fact of the appearance itself. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A verb of something landing or falling into place. It is used of a decree becoming effective, so the clause marks the moment a matter stops being pending and takes effect.
The general word for anything that walks the earth, used of animals and of people alike. Its vagueness is part of why the classical commentators record so many different readings of this ayah.
From the root of certainty rather than of belief. The clause does not say people disbelieved; it says their conviction never became settled, which is a narrower and more exact charge.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The word used here was in daily use for livestock and for anything that moved along the ground. A man's beast was his transport, his capital and sometimes his food. Nothing in the vocabulary is exotic, and that plainness is worth noticing, because an extraordinary event is described with the most ordinary noun available. The classical commentators felt the same gap and said so.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here for a creature brought out of the earth occurs only once in the Quran. Elsewhere the same noun appears dozens of times for ordinary animals, including in surah 34, where it names the small creature that gnawed through the staff Solomon was leaning on. Of this one the Quran gives no description at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A limit is placed on what can be known in advance about the end, and the commentary tradition has largely respected it. What is affirmed is that a moment arrives when the matter stops being open to argument, and that the charge at that point is not ignorance but unsettled conviction. The emphasis falls on certainty rather than on information, which is where this surah has been pressing throughout.

crossReferences.why: Continues directly, using the same phrase about the word falling upon them.
Describes the same unsettled state, people saying they are only guessing about the Hour.
Uses the same noun for the small creature that revealed Solomon's death to the workers.

studies.applyIt: The charge in this ayah is not disbelief but never quite arriving at certainty. Ask which of your convictions you have been holding at that temperature: agreed with, never settled, never acted on. Name one. You do not have to resolve it today. Notice only that you have been treating an open question as though it were closed.

studies.title: Asked Before The Sentence
studies.meaning: A party is gathered from every community, held in ranks, and brought forward. The question put to them has two halves and the first is the sharp one: did you reject the signs without ever having taken them in? Not did you disbelieve, but did you decide before you understood. The second half asks what they were doing instead. Then the sentence falls, and the passage closes by saying they do not speak, which is the only description of them it gives.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the surah's final sequence of scenes from the Day. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. The Meccan opposition held a settled position and had shown no interest in examining the recitation, which is what gives the first half of the question its edge. The scene is not general judgement here but a specific gathering, a delegation drawn out of each community.

keyTerms.note: A group detached from a larger body. The word implies selection, so this is not everyone but a representative party drawn out of each community and brought forward to answer.
A verb for restraining a crowd so the front does not outrun the back. It is used of organising an army on the march, and it turns a mass of people into an order.
From the root for surrounding something. To encompass a thing in knowledge is to have gone all the way round it, which is precisely what the question says they had not done.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Delegations were how Arabia did business. A tribe sent a party to speak for it, and that party's standing, its wording and its reception were all watched closely, because a whole people would be bound by whatever happened in the meeting. Marshalling such a group into order, the front held back until the rest caught up, was an ordinary sight at a court or a great gathering.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing how the group is held in ranks appears three times in the Quran, and one of the others stands in this same surah, at ayah 17, where Solomon's armies of jinn, humans and birds are marshalled in exactly that way. All three occurrences end their ayah with the identical two-word phrase.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The question asked before sentence is passed concerns method rather than conclusion. It does not ask why they refused; it asks whether they had done the work that would make a refusal informed. That is a claim about what an honest rejection would even look like. And the silence at the end is not described as being forbidden to speak, but simply as having nothing left to say.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for being held in ranks as the enemies of God are gathered.
Says they rejected what they had not grasped, before its interpretation had reached them.
Uses the same marshalling verb for Solomon's assembled forces, earlier in this surah.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you dismissed without looking into it. Everyone keeps a shelf of these: a book, a person's argument, an entire field. Spend twenty minutes today actually looking at one of them. You are allowed to end up dismissing it again. The question here is not about the verdict; it is about whether you had earned it.

studies.title: Night To Rest In
studies.meaning: One question, and it concerns something nobody had thought to notice. The night was made so that you could settle in it, and the day was made able to be seen by. The Arabic gives the day the quality of showing rather than of being bright, an unusual construction the commentators remark on. The ayah then calls this a set of signs for people who believe, which narrows the audience in the same breath as it widens the evidence available.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the close of the surah, following several scenes from the Day of Judgement. The placement is deliberate: after the largest possible events, the argument comes back to the smallest and most repeated one. No occasion of revelation is reported. The audience being addressed had never had a night that was not dark, nor a day that was not the working shift.

keyTerms.note: From the root of stillness and of dwelling, which also gives the word for a house. The night is described as somewhere to come to rest rather than as a stretch of unconsciousness.
An active participle, so the day is described as the one doing the seeing rather than as the thing seen. Commentators read it as the day making things visible, a construction the Arabic allows.
The same word used for the verses of this Book. Applying it to the night and the day puts two kinds of evidence on one footing, which the Quran does deliberately and repeatedly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Without lamps that could light a room properly, the day was the working shift and there was no extending it. Caravans travelled at night in summer to escape the heat and by day in winter, and the whole rhythm of trade, prayer and family life ran on a boundary nobody could move. Night was not leisure. It was the only time the body was permitted to stop.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic gives the day an active form, so that the day is doing the seeing rather than being seen. Grammarians have discussed the construction for centuries, and the usual reading is that the day makes things visible for others. It is one of several places where the Quran assigns an action to a stretch of time itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument comes back from cosmic scenes to the most ordinary fact available and calls it a sign, which is a claim about where evidence lives. Nothing rare is being appealed to. And the closing clause is honest about what a sign can accomplish: the alternation is there for everyone, and it functions as a sign for those willing to read it as one, which is why the ayah is a question.

crossReferences.why: States the same pairing, night for rest and day for seeing, as a sign for those who listen.
Names sleep as rest, night as a covering and day as a livelihood, in three short lines.
Calls the night a garment and sleep a repose, and the day a rising.

studies.applyIt: Tonight, notice the moment your body stops arguing and begins to settle. Most people override it and stay up. Just observe it once, without necessarily obeying it. The ayah says the night was made for that settling, which means the pull you feel is not a weakness in you. It is the arrangement doing what it was set up to do.

studies.title: Everyone Comes Brought Low
studies.meaning: The trumpet sounds and terror runs through everything in the heavens and the earth, with one exception the ayah declines to identify: except whom God wills. Commentators record several suggestions and settle on none. Then the sentence closes with everyone arriving in a state named by a single unusual word, meaning brought low and made small. The two halves differ. Fear happens to some and not to others. The arriving lowered happens to all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The trumpet appears across the earliest layers of the recitation, and this is one of four places using this exact phrase for it. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. Its audience knew what a horn sounded like as a signal in war and at gatherings, so the image reached them with a sound attached rather than as an abstraction about the end.

keyTerms.note: The word for a horn blown as a signal. The phrase about it being blown occurs four times in the Quran, and the instrument itself is never described beyond the bare noun.
A sudden startled fear rather than a settled dread. The same root returns two ayat later, where some people are said to be secure from the terror of that day.
Occurs twice in the Quran. It describes arriving in a state of smallness, and here it is applied without exception to everyone, including those who were spared the terror.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A horn was a practical instrument. It called a tribe together, signalled the start of a raid, and carried across country where a voice could not. Everyone had heard one and everyone knew what it did to a camp: activity stopping, heads turning, the whole settlement reorienting to a single sound. The ayah borrows the only technology in that world that could reach everybody at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing how everyone arrives occurs only twice in the Quran. The other place is in surah 40, where it describes those too proud for worship entering the Fire in exactly that state. Here it is said of everyone without exception, which is why the classical commentators read it as a description of creaturely position rather than of punishment.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah separates two things that usually travel together: fear, which is distributed unevenly and by God's choosing, and lowness, which is universal. Being spared the terror does not mean arriving as an equal. That distinction keeps the hope in the passage from hardening into a claim of standing, and it says something about creaturehood that no degree of favour alters.

crossReferences.why: Names those who will be secure from the terror of that day, two ayat later.
Gives the fullest account of the trumpet, with a second blast following the first.
Holds the only other use of the word for arriving brought low.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your day is organised around not appearing small: the tone in the meeting, the answer that was slightly larger than the truth, the effort not to seem uninformed. This ayah says everyone arrives lowered, including those who are safe. Let one of those small performances go today, and see what it actually costs you.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Mountains Passing Like Clouds
studies.meaning: You look at the mountains and take them for set solid, and they are moving, the way clouds move. Commentators divide over the reference: some read it of the Day just described, when the mountains are set going, and others of the world as it stands. The ayah does not adjudicate. It attaches the observation instead to a name for God as the one who made everything precisely, then closes by saying He is aware of what you do, which brings a cosmic sentence down onto conduct.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, placed immediately after the trumpet and before the account of what each person brings with them. The commentators report no occasion for the ayah. Its link with the ayat around it is what shapes the classical discussion, since the sequence is describing the Day while the language of the sentence itself is drawn from ordinary looking at a horizon.

keyTerms.note: Occurs once in the Quran. The root is used of water becoming ice and of anything that has hardened, so the word describes not merely stillness but a stillness assumed to be permanent.
An ordinary verb of passing by, in the present tense. The plainness does the work here: nothing dramatic is claimed, only that a thing you took for stationary is in motion.
Occurs once in the Quran. It means finishing something to exact tolerances, and it is the word an Arabic speaker would reach for about a craftsman whose work has no slack in it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mountains were the fixed points of Arabian geography. Routes were described by them, territory was defined by them, and a poet located a memory by naming the peak it happened under. When everything else in the landscape shifted with the season, the hills did not. Telling that audience the mountains were passing like clouds removed the one thing they measured other things against.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in this ayah occur nowhere else in the Quran: the one for the mountains looking set solid, and the one for making a thing with precision. They stand in the same sentence, so a claim about something merely appearing motionless and a claim about exact workmanship are introduced together and then never used again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah puts perception and reality at a distance from one another and does not treat that as alarming. What looks unchanging is moving, and the fact is offered as evidence of craftsmanship rather than of instability. Then the final clause turns without warning to the reader's own conduct, which places human behaviour inside the same precisely made arrangement rather than outside it looking on.

crossReferences.why: Describes the mountains being set moving among the signs that the Day has begun.
Shows the mountains moved off and the earth left level and entirely exposed.
Pairs the sky in commotion with the mountains travelling, in two short lines.

studies.applyIt: Look at something today that you are sure is not changing: a friendship, a job, an opinion you have held for ten years. Take one and ask what it would look like observed at a different speed. You do not need an answer by the evening. The habit this ayah trains is a small suspicion of the word fixed.

studies.title: Better Than What You Brought
studies.meaning: Two sentences, deliberately unbalanced. Whoever comes with a good thing receives something better than it, and is safe from the terror of that day. Whoever comes with a bad thing has their face tumbled into the fire, and the closing question says only that they are repaid for what they did. The asymmetry is the whole point. The good is met with an increase that is never specified, and the bad is met with exactly itself and nothing added.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the sequence of scenes from the Day.
