These lines appear in similar form in surah 6 and again in the surah that follows this one, where the wording of the first half is nearly identical. No occasion of revelation is reported. The pairing belongs to the earliest and most repeated part of the message, stated to an audience that had already heard it in several shapes.

keyTerms.note: A word for what is beautiful or good, used of a deed and of a blessing alike. Its breadth matters, since the ayah specifies neither a size nor a category of act.
A comparative left deliberately open. Another passage fills it in as tenfold; here nothing is quantified, so what is promised is an increase whose measure is not disclosed at all.
The same word used two ayat earlier of what strikes everything when the trumpet sounds. Here some are said to be secure from it, which identifies the exception left unnamed there.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Bringing something was the ordinary form of a claim. You came to a patron, a court or a market with goods in hand, and what you carried set the terms of what you could ask for. The verb in both halves of this passage is that verb. It pictures the Day as an arrival where each person holds what they have, and nothing else counts for anything.
studies.didYouKnow: The opening phrase, whoever comes with a good deed, appears three times in the Quran: in surah 6, here, and in the surah that immediately follows this one. In surah 6 the reward is stated as tenfold. Here and in the next surah the amount is left open, and the good is simply said to be answered with something better.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two halves are not symmetrical and the passage makes no attempt to balance them. Reward exceeds what was brought; consequence matches it precisely. That imbalance is a statement about how God deals rather than about what people deserve, and the closing question makes the second half self-explanatory. Nothing is added to what was done, which rules out any excess on that side of the account.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same pairing with the increase specified as ten times the deed brought.
Repeats the first half almost exactly in the surah that follows this one.
Names the great terror and says it will not grieve those who are secure.

studies.applyIt: Do one small good thing today that nobody will know about, and notice the impulse to mention it. That impulse is a request for the return to be paid now, in a currency you can see and count. The ayah promises a better return and declines to say what it is. Try, just once, letting it stay unspecified.

studies.title: Lord Of This Town
studies.meaning: The messenger's own instructions are stated in the first person, and there are only two: worship the Lord of this town, and be among those who submit. The town is not named. It is identified as the place He made inviolable, and then the sentence widens at once, since everything belongs to Him. Commentators read the sequence as a correction of local pride. The sanctuary matters because of whose it is, and the one it belongs to is not local at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and aimed at Mecca specifically. The city's standing rested on its sanctuary, which brought it security, pilgrim traffic and trade. The ayah accepts the sanctity and reassigns the credit for it. No occasion of revelation is reported. Its audience were custodians of a shrine whose prestige they had inherited and whose terms they had, in the recitation's account, quietly altered.

keyTerms.note: This definite form occurs once in the Quran. It is the ordinary word for a settled place, so the sanctuary is named by the plainest available description rather than by any title of honour.
From the root of what is set apart and protected. The verb makes the sanctity an act performed upon the place rather than a quality the place possesses on its own account.
The participle from the root of surrender. Placing the messenger among them rather than above them is the whole point of the second half of the sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sanctuary made Mecca work. Inside its boundary blood feuds paused, and tribes fighting elsewhere could trade in the same market. Pilgrims arrived, goods moved, and the families who tended the shrine held their position because of it. A city with no farmland and very little water lived entirely on an arrangement that depended on the place being treated as inviolable.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where the town is named in this particular definite form. Elsewhere the sanctuary is described with different words, and the name of the city itself appears only once in the whole Book. The most important place in the audience's world is identified here by the plainest noun the language offers.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A claim about one particular place is made and then immediately relativised. Yes, this town was made inviolable, and also everything belongs to Him, which means the sanctuary confers no ownership on its custodians. The messenger's role is then defined by two commands he received rather than by any authority he holds, and the second of them puts him inside the community he is calling.

crossReferences.why: Names the security and provision the sanctuary gave this same city, and who supplied them.
Points out that a secure sanctuary was given while people around it were being seized.
Records Abraham asking for this place to be made secure and its people provided for.

studies.applyIt: Think of an advantage you did not earn: where you were born, a language you speak, a name that opens a door. Name one honestly. Then notice how fast the mind converts an inherited advantage into a claim about oneself. This ayah performs that conversion in reverse, in a single clause, and it takes about a second.

studies.title: Guided To Your Own Benefit
studies.meaning: The instructions continue and the third is to recite. Then the consequences divide. Whoever takes the guidance takes it for himself, and whoever goes astray is met not with an argument but with a sentence the messenger is told to say: I am only one of the warners. Commentators read the closing formula as a release. The benefit of guidance accrues to the one guided, and the loss involved in refusing it does not fall on the one who delivered the message.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the very end of the surah, alongside the two commands in the ayah before it. No occasion of revelation is reported. The word for reciting names the activity that had defined the mission for years in Mecca, carried out publicly, at the sanctuary and in the markets, and by that stage at real personal cost to the people doing it.

keyTerms.note: From the root for following, so reciting is described as following the text along rather than performing it. The same root gives the word used throughout for the recitation of signs.
A reflexive form, so the person is the one doing the accepting. The grammar carries the ayah's argument before the explanation arrives in the clause that follows it.
The plural, and the messenger is placed among them rather than singled out. A warner is defined by what he says in advance, not by what happens in the town afterwards.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Warning was a recognised role. A man who saw a raiding party from a hilltop ran down and told the settlement, and the practice had its own conventions, including gestures that signalled urgency at a distance. Everyone knew what a warner was for. He was not answerable for whether the camp moved. He was answerable for arriving in time and for being clear.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah closes with three first person commands given to the messenger: worship the Lord of this town, be among those who submit, and recite. Nothing else is included. The whole mission, at the end of a surah containing kings, armies, jinn and a talking bird, is summed up in three verbs, and not one of them involves persuading anybody.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is described as a benefit belonging to the one who receives it rather than as a service rendered to God or to the messenger. That reframing removes two things at once: any sense that the guided are doing God a favour, and any sense that the messenger has failed when someone refuses. What remains is a task with a clear boundary and consequences that fall where they were earned.

crossReferences.why: States the same division, that guidance is for oneself and straying is against oneself.
Repeats it and adds that you are not a keeper set over them.
Establishes the limit these lines assume, that you cannot make the unwilling listen.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you know is good for you and have been doing partly to satisfy someone else: a habit, a discipline, a course of study. Ask whether you would keep it if that person never noticed again. The ayah says the benefit lands on the person who takes it. It is worth checking whose account you have been posting to.

studies.title: You Will Recognise Them
studies.meaning: The surah closes with praise and a promise. He will show you His signs and you will recognise them: not merely see them, but know them for what they are, which is the thing the whole surah has been arguing does not happen automatically. The final clause is addressed to everyone still listening. Your Lord is not inattentive to what you do. Commentators note that the surah ends on the same word of praise it used at two earlier turning points.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The closing formula answers the objections gathered across the previous ayat without conceding a date, which the surah has already refused to give. No occasion of revelation is reported. The promise of recognition arrives at the end of a surah in which every character who saw a sign had to work out what it meant, from a bird's report to a floor made of glass.

keyTerms.note: Praise given for what someone is as well as for what they have done. The word opens and closes several surahs, and here it appears for the third and final time within this one.
A verb of knowing something again, distinct from learning it for the first time. It implies the signs will be identifiable, which the surah has spent many ayat saying is not guaranteed now.
The word for someone whose attention has drifted from something present. Denying it of God differs from asserting knowledge, since it addresses attention rather than information.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Recognition was a practical skill in a world without documents. You knew a man by his face and his lineage, a camel by its brand, a route by its landmarks. Being able to identify a thing again after an interval was how trade, guarantees and safe passage all worked. The verb that ends this surah is drawn from that world rather than from a philosophical one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word of praise appears three times in this surah, and the three placements mark out its structure: once when David and Solomon are given knowledge, once at the seam where the prophet narratives end and the questions begin, and once here at the close. The same opening phrase occurs more than twenty times across the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah ends by promising recognition rather than argument. Signs will be shown and they will be known, which is a claim about a future clarity rather than a present one, and it lets the disputes recorded through the surah stand unresolved for now. The final clause then closes the gap between that future and the present day, since nothing done in the interval goes unnoticed.

crossReferences.why: Promises the same showing of signs, on the horizons and within themselves, until it becomes clear.
Uses the same opening of praise at the seam between the narratives and the questions.
Denies the same inattention, saying God is not unaware of what wrongdoers do.

studies.applyIt: Look back at one thing from your past that you did not understand at the time and now do. Just one. Notice that nothing about the event itself changed; only your ability to read it did. The surah ends on that promise, and the small version of it has already happened to you more than once.
